design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis (PRISMA; PROSPERO CRD420251062250) of human studies of the health effects of Swedish snus and tobacco-free oral nicotine pouches. PubMed, EMBASE, Scopus and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews were searched up to 25 July 2026, English only, with six search terms (the full strategy is in an online resource that was not read). 2,215 records, 1,241 after duplicates, 102 read in full, 66 studies included: 54 on snus and 15 on pouches (some studies count in both). Results are narrated outcome by outcome, with no pooling and no certainty grading. Study quality was scored with the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) tools and risk of bias rated with CLARITY, NOS-xs and Joanna Briggs Institute tools; per-study ratings are in an online resource that was not read. Biomarker studies, studies of people who use several products, reviews and non-English papers were excluded.
can_establish: What human studies of snus and of tobacco-free nicotine pouches had been published by July 2026 under the review's criteria: how many, of what design, where, and with what follow-up; what each reported for blood pressure, heart rate, metabolic, respiratory, oral, mental-health, cancer, pregnancy and smoking-reduction outcomes; and, above all, how thin the pouch evidence is (15 studies, the longest 6 months, none following disease or death).
cannot_establish: That snus or pouches cause any listed outcome (the review itself says its observational designs prevent causal conclusions); the size of any risk (no pooling, no grading, no absolute risks); how either product compares with smoking for any disease; long-term effects of pouches (none measured); anything about women or about countries outside Scandinavia for snus (most studies are of Swedish and Norwegian men); and independent replication (several cohorts, notably the Swedish construction-worker cohort, feed many of the 66 'studies'). The review's abstract and conclusions say more than its printed estimates show (see reporting issues).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable at review level. Databases: PubMed (330 records), Scopus (638), EMBASE (1,078) and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (169), searched up to 25 July 2026 with 'nicotine pouch', 'tobacco free nicotine pouch', 'oral nicotine pouch', 'snus', 'Swedish moist snuff' and 'health'; no reference-list, register or grey-literature search is described (Methods › Search Strategy; Results › Study Selection, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: controlled, cross-sectional, case-control, cohort, observational and prospective studies of people aged 12 and over who currently or formerly used snus or tobacco-free pouches, reporting acute or chronic health effects, cancer or nicotine dependence, in English. Excluded: letters, commentaries, reviews, protocols, other languages, other products (cigarettes, e-cigarettes, heated tobacco, nicotine gum, sprays, patches), and papers on chemical composition, methods, markets or regulation; at full-text stage, studies of tobacco products in general or smokeless tobacco without separating snus or pouches, studies of people who use several products, and studies of biomarkers of exposure or potential harm (Methods › Eligibility Criteria; Study Selection, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). No list of the 36 studies dropped at full-text stage is given in the page text (Figure 1 is an image and was not read).
sample.demographics: Mostly men in Scandinavia: 40 of 66 studies were set in Sweden and 6 in Norway; many include men only. The 15 pouch studies are five short crossover trials of 30 to 42 adults (four in adults who smoke, one in people who use snus or pouches), a 24-week trial of oral health (n printed as 155; the sex counts sum to 100), an 8-week pilot (n = 45), a 6-month online cohort (n = 1,863 at start), a national cohort (n = 5,556), three cross-sectional surveys in Saudi Arabia (n = 489, 1,214 and 831; where sex is given, almost all men) and three Swedish oral-health studies (n = 23 to 272) (Table 1).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. The review notes that four controlled studies lost more than 20% of participants (Results › Quality of the Studies, 1st paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: English only; four databases; six search terms including 'health'; no grey literature or reference-list search described. Biomarker studies and studies of people who use several products were removed at full-text stage, which removes the studies that most directly compare toxicant exposure from pouches with exposure from cigarettes and the many people who use more than one product. Several of the 66 are reports from the same Swedish cohorts or pooled analyses that contain them (for example the construction-worker cohort appears in Luo 2007, Hergens 2007, Arefalk 2012 and in the pooled analyses of Araghi, Hansson, Hergens and Yang), so '66 studies' overstates independent evidence. The largest pooled mortality analysis of men who use snus (Byhamre 2021, 169,103 men) is not among the included studies; only Byhamre 2017 (metabolic syndrome) is.

exposure.measurement: In primary studies, mostly self-reported use of snus or pouches; the review says all but one observational study relied on self-report, and few measured use more than once (Results › Quality of the Studies, 1st paragraph). In the crossover trials the product and nicotine strength were assigned.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesised. Product content cited in the Introduction from other papers: nicotine 12.8 mg per snus pouch and 1.79 to 47.5 mg per tobacco-free pouch, set beside 1.64 to 2.28 mg per cigarette (Introduction, 2nd paragraph, citing Lawler 2020 and Mallock 2024); the cigarette figure is of a different kind (a per-cigarette quantity of unstated type) and is not comparable with content per pouch. Crossover trials used single exposures of 30 to 60 minutes; the longest pouch follow-up is 6 months. Route: oral.
exposure.polysubstance: People who use several products were excluded at full-text stage, yet included studies enrolled smokers (the pouch switching and craving trials), people who currently or formerly used snus (Alizadehgharib 2026, Rosa 2025) and groups combining snus and pouches (Miluna 2022); some limitations lists note dual use as unmeasured. Attribution of an outcome to the pouch alone is therefore not possible for several of the 15 pouch studies.

comparison.controls: Varies by study: people who never used tobacco in the cohorts; continuing cigarettes in the switching trials; a placebo pouch and nicotine gum in one 9-hour trial; no comparison group in the three Saudi Arabian symptom surveys and in the 6-week plaque study.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not assessed at review level; the Discussion lists diet, exercise, education, income and concurrent tobacco use as possible confounders that differ between studies (Discussion, 1st paragraph).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Smoking is adjusted or restricted in many cohorts; for pouches, smoking history is a design feature of the trials (all enrolled people who smoked) and uncontrolled in the surveys.

outcomes.instruments: Per primary study: blood pressure and heart rate, arterial stiffness, hospital and register diagnoses (heart failure, stroke, diabetes, cancer, pregnancy outcomes), questionnaires (asthma symptoms, mental health, withdrawal and craving scales such as the QSU-Brief), and dental and mucosal examinations.
outcomes.validity_norms: Study quality by NIH tools: controlled studies scored 6 to 12 of 14 ('fair' and 'good'); observational studies 5 to 9 of 14 ('fair'); case-control studies 6 to 8 of 12 ('fair'). Risk of bias mostly moderate, one cross-sectional study high (Results › Quality of the Studies; Risk of Bias). The review states that none of the observational studies justified its sample size or blinded outcome assessors.
outcomes.operationalization: Harm is any association reported in a primary study. The text often calls a non-significant estimate 'increased' or 'reduced' risk (examples in reporting issues), so 'association' in this review does not reliably mean a statistically supported difference.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no pooling). Dozens of outcomes are narrated, each from a handful of studies, with no correction for multiplicity and no weighting by study size.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Both authors screened independently. Who extracted data and who rated quality is not stated in the Methods; the author-contribution statement says both authors analysed the data.

analysis.effect_sizes: Snus, from primary studies as printed in the review (hazard, odds or risk ratios against never use unless stated): heart failure 2.08 (1.03 to 4.22) and 1.28 (1.00 to 1.64) in two cohorts; fatal heart attack in men who never smoked 1.28 (1.06 to 1.55) and non-fatal 0.91 (0.81 to 1.02); pooled acute heart attack 1.04 (0.93 to 1.17); pooled stroke 1.04 (0.92 to 1.17), 1.52 (1.01 to 2.30) for total stroke in people who use snus and never used any tobacco (another cohort); death from cardiovascular disease 1.70 (1.01 to 2.87) in that cohort; hypertension death 1.64 (1.36 to 1.98) and heart-failure death 1.75 (1.17 to 2.62), coronary death 1.10 (0.76 to 1.59) in a cohort of 4,222 men; pooled atrial fibrillation 1.07 (0.97 to 1.19), 1.18 (1.03 to 1.35) in one cohort; type 2 diabetes 1.49 (1.04 to 2.15), 1.15 (1.00 to 1.32), 1.34 (0.65 to 2.7) and 1.00 (0.47 to 2.11) in four studies; asthma 1.49 (1.20 to 1.85); non-affective psychosis 1.22 (1.00 to 1.48), schizophrenia 1.03 (0.70 to 1.54); Parkinson's disease pooled 0.41 (0.28 to 0.61); pancreatic cancer 2.0 (1.2 to 3.3) in the construction-worker cohort against 0.96 (0.83 to 1.11) in a pooled analysis of nine cohorts; rectal cancer 1.40 (1.09 to 1.79) in men who use snus only, colorectal no association; oral cancer 0.90 (0.74 to 1.09) pooled; stillbirth 1.6 (1.1 to 2.3), preterm stillbirth 2.1 (1.3 to 3.4), very preterm birth 1.38 (1.04 to 1.83), intellectual disability in offspring 1.28 (1.06 to 1.52), small for gestational age 1.05 (0.94 to 1.17), preschool asthma or wheeze 1.06 (0.96 to 1.18). Pouches: acute single-use crossover (n = 30), systolic pressure from 1% lower to 3% higher, diastolic 4.5% to 7.4% higher and heart rate from 3% lower to 3.2% higher at 30 minutes, by strength; symptom prevalence in surveys with no comparison group (for example 28.4% rapid or irregular heartbeat, 66.7% bloating); oral lesions 79% and hyperkeratosis 65% among people who use pouches against 89% and 79% among people who use snus (n = 126 and 63); cigarettes per day 15.0 to 8.3 over 8 weeks in a pilot of 45; odds of quitting smoking 1.29 (1.04 to 1.59) for fruit-flavoured and 1.04 (0.82 to 1.28) for mint-flavoured pouches in a 6-month online cohort. No confidence intervals are printed for several results.
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD420251062250 is cited. The article was received on 29 August 2025 and the search ran to 25 July 2026; no deviation from the protocol or search update is described, and the registration was not read.
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract foregrounds adverse associations and omits lower estimates the Results report (Parkinson's disease pooled 0.41, 0.28 to 0.61; reflux in people who use snus daily 0.77, 0.64 to 0.93; hand eczema), which the Discussion does list. No assessment of selective reporting in primary studies.
analysis.power: Not assessed. The review notes that only four controlled studies justified sample size and no observational study did.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 66 studies, mostly cohorts of Swedish men, the estimates for snus are mixed: some are raised with intervals that exclude 1 (heart failure, fatal heart attack, some cohorts' type 2 diabetes, stillbirth and preterm birth, asthma, oral lesions, rectal cancer in men who use snus only), many span 1 (pooled stroke 1.04, atrial fibrillation 1.07, pooled pancreatic cancer 0.96, schizophrenia 1.03, small for gestational age 1.05, preschool asthma 1.06) and some are lower (Parkinson's disease, reflux in daily use, hand eczema). For pouches, 15 studies show small acute blood-pressure and heart-rate changes in single-use crossover trials, symptom surveys without comparison groups, and oral findings in small samples, none longer than 6 months and none following disease or death.
interpretation_gap.claimed: Abstract and Conclusions: current literature 'confirms' negative health consequences of regular snus use, listing increased risk of asthma, atrial fibrillation, hypertension, heart failure, stroke, type 2 diabetes, metabolic disorder, pancreatic and rectal cancer, a weak association with schizophrenia and non-affective disorders, and, after maternal use, small-for-gestational-age births and preschool asthma. The Discussion says pouches increased blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory and gastrointestinal symptoms and oral changes, and that snus use gave no cardiovascular-disease mortality finding. Gaps: (1) atrial fibrillation, stroke, pancreatic cancer (pooled), schizophrenia, small for gestational age and preschool asthma are named as increases though the printed pooled estimates have intervals spanning 1 (or, for schizophrenia, are close to 1); (2) the Discussion's 'no cardiovascular mortality finding' sits beside printed cardiovascular, hypertension and heart-failure death estimates above 1 in the Results; (3) the limitations paragraph says observational designs prevent establishing causality while the Conclusions say the literature 'confirms' harm; (4) respiratory and gastrointestinal 'increases' for pouches come from three Saudi Arabian surveys without comparison groups.

timeline.event: IARC Monograph 100E classifies smokeless tobacco as a class as carcinogenic to humans; it does not mention tobacco-free nicotine pouches.
Pooled analysis of eight Swedish cohorts on mortality in men using snus only (169,103 men); not among the 66 studies of this review.
Systematic review of snus and cancer with graded certainty, which excluded industry-linked studies; reviews were excluded from this review, so it is not cited.
Laboratory comparison of harmful constituents in two nicotine pouch brands with smokeless tobacco and nicotine replacement products; cited in this review's Introduction and Discussion.
Laboratory measurement of nicotine and tobacco-specific nitrosamines across pouch brands; cited in this review's Introduction.

replication.where_it_stands: The only systematic review in this batch that covers both snus and pouches. Its snus sections largely re-narrate Swedish cohorts already covered by the graded 2023 cancer review and the 2021 mortality pool, so they are not independent confirmation, and its abstract is firmer than its estimates. Its pouch inventory, 15 human studies, none longer than 6 months, is its distinctive and most reliable contribution.

funding.funder: Medical University of Lodz, Poland (grant 503/0-149-03/503-01-001), as printed.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare that they have no competing interests.
funding.affiliations_note: Both authors are at the Department of Immunopathology, Faculty of Medicine, Medical University of Lodz. The review does not report who funded the 66 included studies (AMSTAR 2 item 10); only one included trial (Thornley 2009, a 9-hour crossover trial of a pouch against nicotine gum and placebo) is noted in Table 1 as funded by the product's manufacturer. The Discussion calls for tobacco-industry-independent trials of pouches, citing another review. A 2026 scoping review in this batch (Travis) identifies the oral-health trial listed here as Liu 2025 (switching to on! pouches) as Altria-funded, which this review does not say. Recorded as a flag: who funded the other pouch studies could not be checked from the review.

what_would_settle_it: A review with a registered protocol, a justified and wider search (including biomarker studies and people who use more than one product, reported separately), a list of excluded studies, duplicate extraction, funding of included studies and overlapping cohorts tabulated, and results pooled or graded by outcome. For the products themselves: independent, registered cohorts of people who use only pouches or only snus, women included, followed for years, with biomarker and disease outcomes, reported beside people who smoke and people who use no nicotine.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (people aged 12 and over who use snus or pouches), exposure, outcomes and designs are stated, but no comparator is specified; several included designs have none.
PROSPERO CRD420251062250 is cited. No deviations are described, although the manuscript was received in August 2025 and the search ran to July 2026; the registration was not read.
Controlled, cross-sectional, case-control, cohort, observational and prospective designs are listed with no reason for including each.

Four databases and a stated date, but English only without justification, six search terms including 'health', and no reference-list screening, registers, grey literature or experts described. Judged 'no' on the project's reading of item 4 (decision p-amstar2-item4). The full strategy is in Online Resource 1, not read.
Both authors selected independently; disagreements were settled by discussion.
The Methods list the data extracted but do not say that two people extracted or that one checked the other; the contribution statement says both analysed the data.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Counts only (102 read in full, 66 kept). No list of the 36 excluded studies is referenced in the page text; Figure 1 is an image and was not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives design, setting, participants, sample size, measured variables and limitations for each study; exposure (product, brand, amount) and follow-up length are not systematically given, and some entries contain errors (for example 366,381 men with n = 336,381).

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: NIH tools scored every study and CLARITY, NOS-xs and Joanna Briggs tools rated risk of bias, covering confounding, selection and measurement; the Joanna Briggs quasi-experimental checklist was used for 'observational studies', which it was not designed for, and per-study risk ratings are in Online Resource 2 (not read). Overall: mostly moderate.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not tabulated; one manufacturer-funded trial is noted in Table 1's limitations column.
The authors say heterogeneity prevented a meta-analysis (Discussion, 8th paragraph).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Most studies were rated moderate risk and the limitations paragraph says quality was 'not always satisfactory' and that observational designs prevent causal conclusions, but no result is qualified by it and the abstract and Conclusions say the literature 'confirms' harm.

The Discussion attributes inconsistent findings to differences in products, patterns and intensity of use, designs and confounders, and the limitations paragraph lists brand, nicotine and flavour variety.
No quantitative synthesis; publication bias and selective reporting are not discussed.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: University grant stated; no competing interests declared.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: AMSTAR 2 rates three critical items 'no' (the search, the list of excluded studies, and risk of bias in interpretation) and a fourth (the protocol) only partly met, which makes the review critically low confidence: it should not be relied on as an accurate and comprehensive summary of the studies. Item 7 and part of item 9 rest on an online resource and a figure that were not read, but the page text gives no sign of either being enough to change the rating. It may be cited for the inventory it gives (counts, designs, countries, durations, and the statement that pouch evidence is thin and short), for the printed estimates of single studies (to be checked against those studies), and for the limitations its authors state; not for its conclusion that the literature confirms harm, for any claim of direction where the abstract and the printed estimates differ, for any comparison with smoking, or as independent confirmation of the Swedish cohort findings.

key_findings.finding: Search and selection: 2,215 records (PubMed 330, Scopus 638, EMBASE 1,078, Cochrane 169), 1,241 after duplicates, 102 read in full, 66 included; 54 studies on snus and 15 on pouches (some in both); 40 set in Sweden, 8 in the USA, 6 in Norway, 3 in Saudi Arabia, 5 international. Search to 25 July 2026, English only.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Search Strategy, 1st paragraph; Results › Study Selection, 1st paragraph; Results › Study Characteristics, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Quality and risk of bias: controlled studies scored 6 to 12 of 14 on the NIH tool (three open-label, four with more than 20% drop-out, five explaining randomisation); observational studies 5 to 9 of 14 ('fair'), all but one using self-reported snus or pouch use, none justifying sample size or blinding assessors; case-control studies 6 to 8 of 12. Most studies were rated moderate risk of bias; one cross-sectional study was rated high.
key_findings.locator: Results › Quality of the Studies, 1st paragraph; Results › Risk of Bias, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Pouch evidence base (15 studies): five short crossover trials of 30 to 42 adults (blood pressure, heart rate, craving, abuse potential; one 9-hour trial funded by the manufacturer), a 24-week trial of oral health (n printed as 155; sex counts sum to 100), an 8-week pilot (n = 45), a 6-month online cohort (n = 1,863 at start), a national cohort (n = 5,556), three cross-sectional symptom surveys in Saudi Arabia (n = 489, 1,214, 831) and three Swedish oral-health studies (n = 23 to 272). The longest follow-up is 6 months; no study follows disease or death.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Health Effects Associated with Tobacco-Free Oral Nicotine Pouches, all subsections
key_findings.note: Counts of designs are the editors' reading of Table 1.

key_findings.finding: Pouch heart and blood pressure effects: in a single-use crossover study of 30 people who use snus or pouches, changes measured 30 minutes after use were, by strength, systolic pressure -1% (6 mg), +3% (9 mg) and +1.4% (11.2 mg), diastolic +4.5%, +7.4% and +3.9%, and heart rate -3%, +3.2% and -0.2%; in a survey with no comparison group 28.4% of people who use pouches reported rapid or irregular heartbeat.
key_findings.locator: Table 6; Results › Pouches › Cardiovascular System, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The text calls the 11.2 mg product snus and gives its heart-rate change as +0.2%; Table 6 labels it a pouch and gives -0.2%.

key_findings.finding: Pouch symptoms in Saudi Arabian surveys without comparison groups: bloating 66.7%, nausea 47.9%, heartburn 46.7%, difficulty breathing 40.5%, frequent cough or wheeze 27.8%, any psychological effect 39.3%, taste or smell change 36.7%, dry mouth 39.8%.
key_findings.locator: Table 6; Results › Pouches › Gastrointestinal Health, Respiratory System, Oral Health and Mental Health, 1st paragraphs
key_findings.note: Prevalence in people who use pouches only; no estimate of what share of a comparable group without pouches would report the same symptoms.

key_findings.finding: Pouch oral findings: among 272 young Swedish adults, oral lesions 79% and hyperkeratosis 65% in people who use pouches (n = 126) against 89% and 79% in people who use snus (n = 63); erythema 44% and mucosal ulcers 2% in the pouch group; gingival recession 45% against 52%. After 23 dentists switched from snus to pouches, snus lesion severity fell from 95.7% to 69.6% and gingival irritation from 43.5% to 4.3%. In a randomized trial of adults who smoked (n printed as 155), gingival and bleeding indices were 20% to 30% lower at 12 and 24 weeks after switching to pouches than with continued smoking.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pouches › Oral Health, 1st paragraph; Table 6

key_findings.finding: Pouch smoking outcomes: lower urge to smoke than baseline but higher than after a cigarette (QSU-Brief), mixed by strength, in two small crossover trials; higher craving at 5 minutes after pouches (3 mg and 6 mg) than after cigarettes in one; 8-week pilot, cigarettes per day 15.0 to 8.3, one of 12 on pouches quit; 6-month cohort, quitting odds 1.29 (1.04 to 1.59) for fruit-flavoured and 1.04 (0.82 to 1.28) for mint-flavoured pouches; 9-hour trial, odds of temporary abstinence against gum 2.8 (0.8 to 8.1).
key_findings.locator: Results › Pouches › Nicotine Dependence, Smoking Reduction and Cessation, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Snus and the heart: heart failure HR 2.08 (1.03 to 4.22) in 1,076 older men and 1.28 (1.00 to 1.64) in construction workers; fatal heart attack in never-smokers aRR 1.28 (1.06 to 1.55), non-fatal 0.91 (0.81 to 1.02); pooled heart attack 1.04 (0.93 to 1.17); pooled stroke 1.04 (0.92 to 1.17) but death after stroke HR 1.32 (1.08 to 1.61); pooled atrial fibrillation 1.07 (0.97 to 1.19); in people who use snus and never used any tobacco, total stroke 1.52 (1.01 to 2.30) and cardiovascular death 1.70 (1.01 to 2.87); in never-smoking men followed in one cohort, hypertension death 1.64 (1.36 to 1.98), heart-failure death 1.75 (1.17 to 2.62), coronary death 1.10 (0.76 to 1.59), stroke death 1.12 (0.74 to 1.70).
key_findings.locator: Results › Snus › Cardiovascular System, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Snus and diabetes or metabolic disorder: type 2 diabetes 1.49 (1.04 to 2.15), 1.15 (1.00 to 1.32), 1.34 (0.65 to 2.7, ever use), 1.18 (0.48 to 2.9, current use), and 1.00 (0.47 to 2.11) in Swedish and 0.91 (0.75 to 1.10) in Norwegian men; higher odds with higher weekly use in one study; metabolic disorder with high-dose use 1.6 (1.26 to 2.15).
key_findings.locator: Results › Snus › Metabolic Disorders, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Snus and cancer: pancreatic 2.0 (1.2 to 3.3), oral 0.8 (0.4 to 1.7), lung 0.8 (0.5 to 1.3) in the construction-worker cohort; pooled nine cohorts: oral 0.90 (0.74 to 1.09), pancreatic after smoking adjustment 0.96 (0.83 to 1.11), rectal 1.40 (1.09 to 1.79) in men who use snus only, no clear association for colorectal; colon 1.08 (0.91 to 1.29), described as a positive association.
key_findings.locator: Results › Snus › Risk of Cancer Development, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 5

key_findings.finding: Snus, pregnancy and offspring: stillbirth aOR 1.6 (1.1 to 2.3), preterm stillbirth 2.1 (1.3 to 3.4), very preterm birth 1.38 (1.04 to 1.83), moderately preterm 1.25 (1.12 to 1.40), intellectual disability 1.28 (1.06 to 1.52), small for gestational age 1.05 (0.94 to 1.17), preschool asthma or wheeze 1.06 (0.96 to 1.18); offspring asthma 1.94 (1.23 to 3.10) when a parent used snus before conception (children of mean age 9).
key_findings.locator: Results › Snus › Pregnancy Complications and Offspring's Health, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Snus and smoking reduction: in a trial of 150 adults who smoked, cigarettes per day after 8 weeks fell from 15 to 1.5 with complete switching, from 14.7 to 11.7 with partial switching and rose from 14.1 to 15.6 with continued smoking; in a double-blind placebo trial of 319 men, 63.9% against 67.7% halved smoking at 24 weeks (OR 0.81, 0.48 to 1.36), and one-week quit odds at 36 weeks were 2.7 (1.0 to 7.3).
key_findings.locator: Results › Snus › Nicotine Dependence, Smoking Reduction and Cessation, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Authors' stated limitations: many studies of men only; few data on pouches; self-reported use; no meta-analysis because of heterogeneity; most studies from Scandinavia and Swedish snus differs from products elsewhere; observational designs prevent establishing causality; brands, nicotine content and flavours vary; quality 'not always satisfactory'. Conclusion: too little data to clearly determine the health effects of pouches.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract lists a 'weak association' of snus with schizophrenia and non-affective disorders; the text gives schizophrenia aHR 1.03 (0.70 to 1.54) and non-affective psychosis aHR 1.22 (1.00 to 1.48).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Abstract; Results › Snus › Mental Health, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract overstates a null schizophrenia result.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract names atrial fibrillation, stroke and pancreatic cancer as increased with snus use. The pooled atrial fibrillation estimate is 1.07 (0.97 to 1.19), the pooled stroke estimate 1.04 (0.92 to 1.17) and the pooled pancreatic estimate 0.96 (0.83 to 1.11); the raised estimates come from single cohorts. The text describes colon cancer HR 1.08 (0.91 to 1.29) as a positive association and oral and lung cancer RR 0.8 (0.4 to 1.7; 0.5 to 1.3) as reduced risk.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Abstract; Results › Snus › Cardiovascular System, 3rd paragraph; Risk of Cancer Development, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: Directions are asserted where intervals span 1; the abstract cannot be cited for these outcomes.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says maternal snus use increased the risk of a newborn small for gestational age and of asthma in preschool age; the text gives 1.05 (0.94 to 1.17) and 1.06 (0.96 to 1.18). The one significant asthma result (1.94, 1.23 to 3.10) is for school-age children of parents who used snus before conception.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Abstract; Results › Snus › Pregnancy Complications and Offspring's Health, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Null results are reported as increases in the abstract.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says snus use gave no cardiovascular-disease mortality finding, but the Results print cardiovascular death HR 1.70 (1.01 to 2.87), hypertension death 1.64 (1.36 to 1.98) and heart-failure death 1.75 (1.17 to 2.62), and fatal heart attack 1.28 (1.06 to 1.55).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Discussion, 1st paragraph; Results › Snus › Cardiovascular System, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: The Discussion and Results disagree; the Results numbers are the better guide.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion lists a reduced risk of rheumatoid arthritis among people who use snus; the Results give OR 1.0 (0.8 to 1.2) for developing rheumatoid arthritis and only lower disease activity scores among people who already had it.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Discussion, 1st paragraph; Results › Snus › Autoimmune Disorders, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: A null risk result is reported as a reduction.

reporting_issues.issue: Respiratory and gastrointestinal 'increases' attributed to pouches come from symptom surveys with no comparison group; blood-pressure 'increases' come from one crossover study whose changes run from -1% to +3% (systolic) by strength. Oral mucosal findings in Miluna 2022 are from snus and pouches analysed as one group.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Table 1 (Miluna 2022); Table 6
reporting_issues.consequence: The Discussion's statement that pouches increased these outcomes is not supported by comparisons in the studies reviewed.

reporting_issues.issue: In the snus cardiovascular text the 11.2 mg product in Renard 2025 is called snus and its 30-minute changes are given as systolic +1.4%, diastolic +3.9% and heart rate +0.2%; Table 6 gives the same systolic and diastolic figures for 'Nordic Spirit 11.2 mg ONP' with a heart-rate change of -0.2%. A scoping review in this batch describes a five-product study in people who use snus that appears to be the same study, with both an 11.2 mg pouch and an 11.2 mg snus.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Results › Snus › Cardiovascular System, 1st paragraph; Table 6
reporting_issues.consequence: The same numbers are attributed to two different products and the sign of the heart-rate change differs; the primary paper was not read.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints 366,381 men with n = 336,381 for Nordenvall 2011, n = 155 for Liu 2025 with 44 men and 56 women (100), and n = 489 for Aldali 2026 with 381 men and 14 women (395); the text cites Munafo 'et al. 2007' for a study listed as 2016. The three quality tables list 67 appraisals against 66 included studies because Rasouli 2017 (a Swedish case-control and a Norwegian cross-sectional study) is appraised twice.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 1; Tables 3 and 4; Results › Snus › Mental Health, 1st paragraph; Results › Quality of the Studies, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical errors with no effect on the findings.

reporting_issues.issue: The Introduction sets nicotine per pouch (12.8 mg snus; 1.79 to 47.5 mg tobacco-free pouches) beside 1.64 to 2.28 mg per cigarette.
reporting_issues.consequence: Content per pouch and a per-cigarette quantity of unstated kind are not comparable; use Mallock 2024 for the pouch measurements.
